analysis.one_liner: Replaces the House's self-policing ethics committee with an independent commission and requires quarterly, free online lobbying disclosures.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in three House committees until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have abolished the House Committee on Standards of Official Conduct — the committee made up of House members that polices other House members — and replaced it with an 11-member Independent Ethics Commission made up of former House members, with bans on recent members and registered lobbyists serving on it [S2][S3]. The Commission would investigate misconduct by members, officers, and employees of the House, take over lobbyist registration and enforcement from the Clerk of the House and Secretary of the Senate, and require lobbyists to file disclosure reports every three months in electronic form, posted online free of charge [S2][S3]. House leaders would print and act on Commission recommendations within set time limits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want to see who is lobbying Congress: the bill required quarterly lobbying reports filed electronically and posted on the Internet at no charge, instead of the twice-yearly filings then in place [S2][S3]. It also aimed to give House misconduct investigations a body whose members were not current House members, by requiring commissioners to be former House members barred from recent service or registered lobbying [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Lobbying disclosure reports would be filed quarterly rather than semiannually, in electronic form, and made available to the public over the Internet without a fee within 30 days of filing [S2][S3].
The Commission would cross-check all reports filed by House members, officers, employees, and lobbyists for inconsistencies and mutual financial interests between them [S3].

The Commission could investigate alleged violations of conduct rules by any member, officer, or employee of the House and issue letters of reproval, with its findings printed in the Congressional Record and acted on by the House within 30 days [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Registered lobbyists would bear more frequent and more public reporting. Incumbent House members would give up direct control of ethics enforcement, since the member-run Standards Committee would be abolished and investigations handled by an outside commission [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill kept insider control at the top: the Speaker and minority leader would appoint all 11 commissioners, and every member had to be a former House representative, so a closed circle of ex-lawmakers would police the current one [S3].

Public access to the process was limited: a complaint from someone who is not a House member could only be investigated after being submitted to at least three members who refused in writing to transmit it, and no complaint information could be disclosed without a vote of the full Commission [S3].
No investigation could be started, and no finding issued, without approval of a majority of the 11 commissioners, a higher bar than the old committee faced [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The lobbying-disclosure improvements — quarterly, electronic, free-to-read filings — were real, concrete gains for public transparency. But the core swap, replacing a member-run ethics committee with a commission of former members appointed by the two House leaders, was a modest change in who watches Congress rather than a truly independent watchdog, and the complaint and disclosure rules kept much of the process behind closed doors. A well-designed bill would have gone further on independence and public complaint access.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees in March 2006, and none of them ever took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer, joined by Rep. Greg Walden of Oregon, introduced the bill on March 14, 2006 [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the Committee on House Administration and, in addition, to the Rules and Judiciary Committees [S1][S5].

The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action of any kind after the referral; the next recorded event would have been in a later Congress, and none came before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: House incumbents kept ethics enforcement in their own hands through the Committee on Standards of Official Conduct, and registered lobbyists kept the slower, less public semiannual filing system. Nothing about the bill advanced beyond a referral, so no one had to defend it on the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican cosponsor from his own Oregon delegation, giving it 2 cosponsors split evenly between the parties, but no vote ever occurred to show where the broader chambers stood.

industries.industry: Registered lobbying firms and their clients
industries.note: The bill would have moved them from twice-yearly filings to quarterly electronic reports posted online free of charge, making their influence activity far more visible to voters. The current, less frequent system stayed in place because the bill never advanced [S2][S3].

The bill would have abolished the member-run Committee on Standards of Official Conduct and moved investigations to a commission of former members, taking discipline of sitting members out of their own hands. Members kept that control because the bill never got a hearing [S2][S3].
Only former House representatives were eligible for the commission, so the bill would have created a new paid role reserved for ex-lawmakers — an insider channel even inside a reform bill [S3].
